{{Short description|Circle packing arranged in spirals}}
[[File:PSM V79 D459 Logarithmic spiral in flower growth configuration.png|thumb|upright=1.3|A Doyle spiral of type (8,16) printed in 1911 in ''[[Popular Science]]'' as an illustration of [[phyllotaxis]].{{r|emch}} One of its spiral arms is shaded.|alt=Refer to caption]]
In the mathematics of [[circle packing theorem|circle packing]], a '''Doyle spiral''' is a pattern of non-crossing circles in the plane in which each circle is surrounded by a ring of six [[tangent circles]]. These patterns contain spiral arms formed by circles linked through opposite points of tangency, with their centers on [[logarithmic spiral]]s of three different shapes.

Doyle spirals are named after mathematician [[Peter G. Doyle]], who made an important contribution to their mathematical construction in the late 1980s or {{nowrap|early 1990s.{{r|doyle}}}} However, their study in [[phyllotaxis]] (the mathematics of plant growth) dates back to the early {{nowrap|1900s.{{r|emch|lem|phyll}}}}

==Definition==
A Doyle spiral is defined to be a certain type of [[circle packing]], consisting of infinitely many circles in the plane, with no two circles having overlapping interiors. In a Doyle spiral, each circle is enclosed by a ring of six other circles. The six surrounding circles are tangent to the central circle and to their two neighbors in the {{nowrap|ring.{{r|bds|consym}}}}

==Properties==
===Radii===
As Doyle {{nowrap|observed,{{r|doyle}}}} the only way to pack circles with the combinatorial structure of a Doyle spiral is to use circles whose radii are also highly {{nowrap|structured.{{r|bds}}}} Six circles can be packed around a circle of radius <math>r</math> if and only if there exist three positive real numbers {{nowrap|<math>a</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>b</math>,}} {{nowrap|and <math>c=\tfrac{b}{a}</math>,}} so that the surrounding circles have radii (in cyclic order)
{{bi|left=1.6|<math>ra</math>, <math>rb</math>, <math>rc</math>, <math>r/a</math>, <math>r/b</math>, and <math>r/c</math>.}}
Only certain triples of numbers {{nowrap|<math>a</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>b</math>,}} {{nowrap|and <math>c=\tfrac{b}{a}</math>}} come from Doyle spirals; others correspond to systems of circles that eventually overlap each {{nowrap|other.{{r|consym|intro}}}}

===Arms===
[[File:St Albans cathedral (15080601612).jpg|thumb|Two concentric rings of nine circles in the [[rose window]] of [[St Albans Cathedral]].{{r|archeng}} These two rings are part of a (9,9) Doyle spiral, but the center circle and other circles do not follow the pattern.|alt=Refer to caption]]
In a Doyle spiral, one can group the circles into connecting chains of circles through opposite points of tangency. These have been called ''arms'', following the same terminology used for {{nowrap|[[Spiral galaxy|spiral galaxies]].{{r|cusp|sutcliffe}}}} Within each arm, the circles have radii in a doubly infinite [[geometric sequence]]
<math display=block>\dots, ra^{-2}, ra^{-1}, r, ra, ra^2, \dots</math>
or a sequence of the same type with common multiplier <math>b</math> {{nowrap|or <math>c</math>.}} In most Doyle spirals, the centers of the circles on a single arm lie on a [[logarithmic spiral]], and all of the logarithmic spirals obtained in this way meet at a single central point. Some Doyle spirals instead have concentric circular arms (as in the stained glass window shown) or straight {{nowrap|arms.{{r|consym}}}}

===Counting the arms===
The precise shape of any Doyle spiral can be parameterized by three [[natural number]]s, counting the number of arms of each of its three shapes. When one shape of arm occurs infinitely often, its count is defined as 0, rather {{nowrap|than <math>\infty</math>.}} The smallest arm count equals the difference of the other two arm counts, so any Doyle spiral can be described as being of {{nowrap|type <math>(p,q)</math>,}} where <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are the two largest counts, in the sorted order {{nowrap|<math>p\le q</math>.<ref>{{harvtxt|Beardon|Dubejko|Stephenson|1994}}, Table I, p. 61</ref>}}

{{Multiple image|
|image3=Doyle spiral (6,8) with spirals colored part1.svg|caption3=8 arms
|alt3=Refer to caption
|image2=Doyle spiral (6,8) with spirals colored part2.svg|caption2=6 arms
|alt2=Refer to caption
|image1=Doyle spiral (6,8) with spirals colored part3.svg|caption1=2 arms
|alt1=Refer to caption
|footer=Counting the arms of each type in a spiral of type (6,8)
|total_width=840
|align=center
|caption_align=center
}}

Every pair <math>(p,q)</math> with <math>1<q/2\le p\le q</math> determines a Doyle spiral, with its third and smallest arm count equal to <math>q-p</math>. The shape of this spiral is determined uniquely by these counts, up to {{nowrap|[[Similarity (geometry)|similarity]].{{r|bds}}}} For a spiral of {{nowrap|type <math>(p,q)</math>,}} the radius multipliers are {{nowrap|<math>a = |\alpha|</math>,}} {{nowrap|<math>b = |\beta|</math>,}} {{nowrap|and <math>c = \tfrac{b}{a}</math>}} for complex numbers <math>\alpha</math> and <math>\beta</math> satisfying the coherence equation {{nowrap|<math>\alpha^p = \beta^q</math>}} and the tangency equations
<math display="block">
\frac{1 + |\alpha|}{|1 - \alpha|}
= \frac{1 + |\beta|}{|1 - \beta|}
= \frac{|\alpha| + |\beta|}{|\alpha - \beta|}.
</math>
This implies that the radius multipliers are [[algebraic number]]s.{{r|cusp|intro}} The self-similarities of a spiral centered on the origin form a [[discrete group]] generated by {{nowrap|<math>z \mapsto \alpha z</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math>z \mapsto \beta z</math>.{{r|intro}}}} A circle whose center is distance <math>d</math> from the central point of the spiral has radius {{nowrap|<math>\tfrac{|1 - \alpha|}{1 + |\alpha|}d</math>.{{r|cusp}}}}

Exact values of these parameters are known for a few simple cases. In other cases, they can be accurately approximated by a numerical search, and the results of this search can be used to determine numerical values for the sizes and positions of all of the {{nowrap|circles.{{r|bds|cusp}}}}

===Symmetry===
[[File:Doyle spiral (6,8) under Möbius transformation.svg|thumb|Doyle spiral (6,8) under a [[Möbius transformation]]. The pattern of tangencies is preserved but the three outermost circles are not surrounded by their ring of tangent circles.|alt=Refer to caption]]
Doyle spirals have symmetries that combine scaling and rotation around the central point (or translation and rotation, in the case of the regular hexagonal packing of the plane by unit circles), taking any circle of the packing to any other circle.{{r|consym}} Applying a [[Möbius transformation]] to a Doyle spiral preserves the shape and tangencies of its circles. Therefore, a Möbius transformation can produce additional patterns of non-crossing tangent circles, each tangent to six others. These patterns typically have a double-spiral pattern in which the connected sequences of circles spiral out of one center point (the image of the center of the Doyle spiral) and into another point (the image of the [[point at infinity]]). However, these do not meet all of the requirements of Doyle spirals: some circles in this pattern will not be surrounded by their six neighboring {{nowrap|circles.{{r|cusp|coxlox}}}}

==Examples and special cases==
[[File:Coxeter circles.png|thumb|[[Coxeter's loxodromic sequence of tangent circles]], a Doyle spiral of type (2,3)|alt=Refer to caption]]
The most general case of a Doyle spiral has three distinct radius multipliers, all different {{nowrap|from 1,}} and three distinct arm counts, all nonzero. An example is [[Coxeter's loxodromic sequence of tangent circles]], a Doyle spiral of type (2,3), with arm counts 1, 2, and 3, and with multipliers {{nowrap|<math>\alpha=\tau^3</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math>\beta=\tau^2</math>}} for
<math display="block">\tau=-(1 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\varphi}}) + i(1 + \sqrt{\varphi}),</math>
where <math>\varphi</math> denotes the [[golden ratio]]. Within the single spiral arm of tightest curvature, the circles in Coxeter's loxodromic sequence form a sequence whose radii are powers of <math>|\tau| = \varphi + \sqrt{\varphi}</math>. Every four consecutive circles in this sequence are {{nowrap|tangent.{{r|coxlox}}}}

When exactly one of the three arm counts is zero, the arms that it counts are circular, with radius {{nowrap|multiplier 1.}} The number of circles in each of these circular arms equals the number of arms of each of the other two types. All the circular arms are concentric, centered where the spiral arms {{nowrap|meet.{{r|bds}}}} The multipliers for a Doyle spiral of type {{nowrap|<math>(p,p)</math>}} are {{nowrap|<math>\alpha=a e^{i \frac{\pi}{p}}</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math>\beta=a e^{-i \frac{\pi}{p}}</math>}}.{{r|cusp}}{{efn|Here <math>a = w + \sqrt{w^2 - 1}</math> for <math>w = \tan^2 \tfrac{\pi}{p} + \sec \tfrac{\pi}{p}</math>.{{r|cusp}}}} In the photo of a stained glass church window, the two rings of nine circles belong to a Doyle spiral of this form, of {{nowrap|type (9,9).}}

Straight arms are produced for arm counts {{nowrap|<math>p=q/2</math>.}} In this case, the two spiraling arm types have the same radius multiplier, and are mirror reflections of each other. There are twice as many straight arms as there are spirals of either type. Each straight arm is formed by circles with centers that lie on a ray through the central {{nowrap|point.{{r|bds}}}} Because the number of straight arms must be even, the straight arms can be grouped into opposite pairs, with the two rays from each pair meeting to form a line. The multipliers for a Doyle spiral of type {{nowrap|<math>(p,2p)</math>}} are {{nowrap|<math>\alpha=b^2</math>}} and {{nowrap|<math>\beta=b e^{i \frac{\pi}{p}}</math>}}.{{r|cusp}}{{efn|Here <math>b = \frac{1 + \sqrt{v - c}}{v}</math> for <math>v = \frac{\sqrt{5 + 4c} - 1}{2}</math> and <math>c = \cos \tfrac{\pi}{p}</math>.{{r|cusp}}}} The Doyle spiral of type (8,16) from the ''Popular Science'' illustration is an example, with eight arms spiraling the same way as the shaded arm, another eight reflected arms, and sixteen rays.

[[File:Circle packing (hexagonal).svg|thumb|upright|Hexagonal packing of unit circles|alt=Refer to caption]]
A final special case is the Doyle spiral of type (0,0), a regular hexagonal packing of the plane by unit circles. Its radius multipliers are all one and its arms form parallel families of lines of three different {{nowrap|slopes.{{r|bds}}}}

==Applications==
The Doyle spirals form a discrete analogue of the [[exponential function]], as part of the more general use of circle packings as discrete analogues of [[conformal map]]s. Indeed, patterns closely resembling Doyle spirals (but made of tangent shapes that are not circles) can be obtained by applying the exponential map to a scaled copy of the regular hexagonal circle {{nowrap|packing.{{r|bds}}}} The three ratios of radii between adjacent circles, fixed throughout the spiral, can be seen as analogous to a characterization of the exponential map as having fixed {{nowrap|[[Schwarzian derivative]].{{r|consym}}}} Doyle spirals have been used to study [[Kleinian group]]s, discrete groups of symmetries of [[hyperbolic space]], by embedding these spirals onto the sphere at infinity of hyperbolic space and lifting the symmetries of each spiral to symmetries of the space {{nowrap|itself.{{r|cusp}}}}

Spirals of tangent circles, often with [[Fibonacci number]]s of arms, have been used to model [[phyllotaxis]], the spiral growth patterns characteristic of certain plant species, beginning with the work of [[Gerrit van Iterson]] {{nowrap|in 1907.{{r|phyll}}}} In this context, an arm of the Doyle spiral is called a [[parastichy]] and the arm counts of the Doyle spiral are called ''parastichy numbers''. When the two parastichy numbers <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> are [[Fibonacci numbers]], and either consecutive or separated by only one Fibonacci number, then the third parastichy number will also be a Fibonacci {{nowrap|number.{{r|jdp}}}} With this application in mind, [[Arnold Emch]] in 1910 calculated the positions of circles in Doyle spirals of {{nowrap|type <math>(p,2p)</math>,}} noting in his work the connections between these spirals, logarithmic spirals, and the exponential {{nowrap|function.{{r|emch|lem}}}} For modeling plant growth in this way, spiral packings of tangent circles on surfaces other than the plane, including [[cylinder]]s and [[cone]]s, may also be {{nowrap|used.{{r|growth}}}}

Spiral packings of circles have also been studied as a decorative motif in {{nowrap|[[architectural design]].{{r|archeng}}}}

==Related patterns==
[[File:Sunflower spiral.png|thumb|upright=1.2|Non-Doyle spiral patterns obtained by placing unit circles at equal angular offsets on [[Fermat's spiral]]; the central image is the one with golden-ratio angular offsets|alt=Refer to caption]]
Tangent circles can form spiral patterns whose local structure resembles a square grid rather than a hexagonal grid, which can be continuously transformed into Doyle {{nowrap|packings.{{r|jdp}}}} The space of locally-square spiral packings is infinite-dimensional, unlike Doyle spirals, which can be determined by a constant number of parameters.{{r|square}} It is also possible to describe spiraling systems of overlapping circles that cover the plane, rather than non-crossing circles that pack the plane, with each point of the plane covered by at most two circles except for points where three circles meet at <math>60^\circ</math> angles, and with each circle surrounded by six others. These have many properties in common with the Doyle {{nowrap|spirals.{{r|cover}}}}

The Doyle spiral should not be confused with [[Fermat's spiral#The golden ratio and the golden angle|a different spiral pattern of circles]], studied for certain forms of plant growth such as the seed heads of [[sunflower]]s. In this pattern, the circles are of unit size rather than growing logarithmically, and are not tangent. Instead of having centers on a logarithmic spiral, they are placed on [[Fermat's spiral]], offset by the [[golden angle]] <math>2\pi/\varphi^2\approx 137.5^\circ</math> from each other relative to the center of the spiral, where <math>\varphi</math> is the {{nowrap|[[golden ratio]].{{r|viscomp|sunflower}}}}
